extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians, and computer scientists interested in formal verification, automated reasoning, and the nature of mathematical understanding
extracted.subtask_description: A conceptual/phil osophical account of what it is to understand mathematics, giving task-based abilities, norms for diagram use, criteria for inference and concept mastery, and considerations about complexity and methods (relevant to formal verification, pedagogy, and cognitive science).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding mathematical conventions regarding domains and types
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding mathematical conventions regarding domains and types involves being able to resolve ambiguities and infer type information from the context; being able to recognize concrete domains as implicitly embedded in other domains; being able to recognize concrete and abstract structures as instances of more general classes of structures; and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion bundles several related abilities: (a) resolve ambiguous expressions by inferring appropriate domain/type from context, (b) recognize embeddings (e.g. integers ⊂ rationals ⊂ reals) and when one domain is being used inside another, and (c) spot when an object is an instance of a more general structure (e.g. a group viewed as an instance of a monoid). These skills are required for correct parsing, for switching viewpoints (field vs vector space vs algebra), and for mechanized systems to mirror human mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize multiple views/instances of the same mathematical object
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic reasoning often requires us to view the same object in multiple ways. For example, if F is a field with a subfield E, then F can simultaneously be viewed as a field, a vector space over E, and an algebra over E. If H and K are subsets of a group G that are closed under the group operations, then H and K are also groups in their own right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence requires the ability to switch between and exploit these different perspectives (set, structure, module, subgroup, etc.), and to understand the consequences of each viewpoint (e.g. what operations and properties are available under each). Proof assistants and formal systems need mechanisms to support and reason about such multiple views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding mathematical inference (task-based capability to carry out inferences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding mathematics involves being able to carry out straightforward mathematical inferences in specific mathematical domains, even when those inferences are difficult to spell out in formal axiomatic terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes familiarity with different algorithmic and heuristic approaches: decision procedures (guaranteed termination on certain classes), search procedures (may not halt), domain-general methods (propositional/first-order/higher-order/equality reasoning), domain-specific methods (e.g. linear arithmetic solvers, Groebner-basis methods), and hybrids (combining procedures, Nelson–Oppen style). It also entails recognizing when a principled (completeness-guaranteed) method is feasible versus when heuristic, tinkered methods are more practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish domain-general vs domain-specific and principled vs heuristic methods
rubrics_metrics.description: One can distinguish between decision procedures and search procedures; between methods that are domain-general and methods that are domain-specific; and between 'principled' search methods (that guarantee completeness) and 'heuristic' methods (engineered for practical performance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider which kind of method is appropriate for the target inference: whether one needs guarantees of termination/correctness, or practical heuristics that perform well on typical mathematical problems. The trade-offs (theoretical guarantees vs empirical effectiveness) are central to assessing automated reasoning approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding mathematical diagram use
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding mathematical diagram use involves being able to represent information in a diagram appropriately, and draw valid inferences from the information so represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires knowledge of the implicit norms and conventions governing diagrammatic inferences (what can be 'read off' the diagram and what must be justified formally). Example: Euclid's proofs often read topological facts (inclusion of angles, betweenness) from the diagram without explicit justification, while metric congruences are proved in text. A competent reasoner must (a) represent diagrammatic information faithfully, (b) know which diagrammatic inferences are legitimate under the conventions, and (c) be able to make informal diagram-based claims rigorous when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to distinguish valid from invalid diagrammatic inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding Euclidean geometry means, in part, being able to distinguish the valid diagrammatic inferences from invalid ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should check whether one can justify informal diagrammatic claims (e.g. 'one angle properly contains another') by extracting topological/relational facts from the construction (betweenness, same-side relations, containment) rather than relying on purely visual intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding mathematical concepts as collections of abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concepts can be analyzed as collections of abilities bundled around a central token; for example, understanding the group concept involves a cluster of abilities rather than just knowing a definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete abilities constituting concept-understanding include: (a) stating the definition and applying it correctly, (b) knowing common examples, (c) recognizing implicit instances in other contexts, (d) constructing new instances or deriving structures from others, (e) distinguishing subtypes (abelian, nilpotent, finite/infinite), and (f) knowing relevant theorems and when to apply them. Evaluations of concept mastery should probe across these abilities, not merely test definitional recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task-based components of mathematical understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Doing mathematics means undertaking various tasks (solving problems, proving theorems, verifying inferences, developing theories, forming conjectures); 'understanding' consists of the methods, techniques, procedures, protocols, tactics, and strategies that make this passage possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical rubric for understanding should examine whether an agent can: (a) recognize the nature of the objects and questions before them, (b) marshal relevant background knowledge and information, (c) traverse the space of possibilities in a fruitful way (search strategies, heuristics), and (d) identify contextual features that reduce complexity. These subskills are compositional: higher-level abilities often build on lower-level ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to select and apply methods that manage complexity and make mathematics 'easy'
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding why certain mathematical developments are valuable often hinges on how the right concepts and methods simplify the tasks before us, thereby reducing complexity in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion emphasizes pragmatic measures of ease/difficulty (time, cognitive workload, conceptual streamlining) over purely formal measures (proof length, asymptotic complexity). Good evaluations check whether methods/concepts meaningfully reduce the cognitive and organizational burdens of problem-solving in real mathematical contexts, not merely produce formal speedups in contrived settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciating limits of foundational reduction and importance of higher-level organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Foundational reduction (e.g. everything as sets) washes out distinctions between algebraic and geometric methods, styles of proof, and the value of good definitions; understanding requires attention to higher-level organization and representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments and system designs should favor representations and methods that preserve the structure and conceptual resources mathematicians actually use, because these often make reasoning tractable and meaningful despite the existence of a universal set-theoretic encoding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developing objective, cognition-relative accounts of mathematical value-judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: To make judgments about 'naturalness' or the value of a representational choice objective, we should idealize cognitive capacities and show how certain choices extend the capacity for mathematical use and discovery under constraints like limited time, memory, and attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This suggests a criterion for assessing mathematical practices: do they, under plausible assumptions about human cognitive limits, reliably improve tractability, discoverability, or communicability? Evaluations should therefore relate methods/conventions to modeled cognitive constraints rather than treating such judgments as purely aesthetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to combine and integrate multiple reasoning procedures effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Research has explored combining domain-specific procedures into general frameworks for proof search (e.g. Nelson–Oppen methods); effective mathematical competence includes integrating multiple methods when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rubric should measure whether an agent can orchestrate heterogeneous tools (decision procedures, algebraic methods, search heuristics, computer algebra) in a way that leverages their strengths and controls interactions (e.g. handling overlapping theories), rather than only applying a single isolated method.
